newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury's Summers retracts estate tax remark.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury's Summers retracts estate tax remark.

text.p: Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers on Wednesday retracted a controversial statement he made this week about Congressional "selfishness" in wanting to roll back inheritance taxes.
"I should not have used the term selfishness to characterize positions in the debate over estate taxes," Summers said in a brief meeting with reporters.
On Monday, he told another group of reporters that he considered a bid in Congress to make a reduction in inheritance taxes part of a federal budget agreement was motivated by selfishness.
Summers' remarks drew fire on Tuesday from Senate Majority leader Trent Lott who suggested it might make it more difficult to reach a comprehensive budget pact.

"It is not constructive to have a sub-cabinet level official using the word 'selfish' to describe supporters of death tax reform at a time when we're trying to forge a bipartisan budget agreement with the Prtesident," Lott said in a prepared statement.
In response to a question, Summers denied he was responding directly to Lott's criticism but said he had been "wrong to question the motives of others in policy and policy debate."
"There is room for honest disagreement on this issue," Summers said. "I believe that repeal of the estate tax raises very important questions of cost and fairness."
Summers said the White House's budget proposals contain proposals to deal with "some of the serious and legitimate questions that current estate tax rules pose for small businessmen and farmers."

Current law exempts from taxes the estates of taxpayers whose assets are valued at less than $600,000 when they die. One bipartisan Senate bill last month proposed raising the current estate tax exemption by $400,000 to $1 million.
But Summers said on Monday that was a disproportionate benefit for the rich and suggested that revenues were most easily raised for the government by taxing those with the ability to pay.
